item.research_question: What distinguishes multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) from traditional solid solutions, and how does local chemical order (LCO) influence dislocation behavior and mechanical strength?
item.processing_route: Hybrid molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations with annealing temperatures (Ta) ranging from 650 K to 1650 K; empirical embedded-atom method (EAM) potential developed without spin polarization; simulation box ~52 nm × 6 nm × 52 nm with 1,584,000 atomic sites; 270,000–500,000 MC cycles for convergence.
item.test_conditions: Energy pathway calculations at 0 K; dislocation motion simulations at 300 K under constant shear stress of 300 MPa; strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 for CRSS estimation; activation barrier calculations via minimum energy path (MEP).
key_findings: Configurational entropy (Sc) rarely reaches the ideal value (Sc,ideal); at 1650 K, Sc is ~95% of Sc,ideal, but drops significantly as LCO develops at lower Ta.
Complex stacking fault energy (CSFE) varies from -24.0 mJ/m² (random solid solution) to ~57 mJ/m² (strong LCO at 650 K).
Local antiphase boundary energies (APBEs) increase from ~50 mJ/m² to ~112 mJ/m² as Ta decreases from 1650 K to 650 K.
Twin boundary energy (γB) in LCO samples increases linearly with the number of transformed layers (λ), unlike elemental FCC metals where it converges.
Dislocations move via intermittent nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) rather than smooth propagation, with effective barriers of ~0.15 eV even at 400 MPa shear stress.
Shear stress required to drive dislocation motion increases by a factor of three when the alloy is annealed at 650 K compared to the random state.
Critical resolved shear strength (CRSS) for the random NiCoCr state is ~70 MPa at 300 K and 10^-3 s^-1, consistent with experimental values of ~69 ± 3 MPa.
item.mechanism: LCO creates a rugged energy landscape with spatially heterogeneous complex stacking fault energies (CSFE) and antiphase boundary energies (APBE). This heterogeneity acts as nanoscale obstacles that trap dislocation segments, forcing them to move via a nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) mechanism. The energy required to break LCOs during slip and twinning increases activation barriers and lattice friction, leading to strengthening.
item.limitations: The study uses a non-magnetic EAM potential which does not explicitly consider spin polarization; magnetic effects could alter energy differences by ~15 meV/atom. The simulations assume a single-phase solution without second-phase precipitation. Kinetic limitations in experiments may prevent the formation of predicted LCO states at low temperatures within typical homogenization times.
item.future_work: The authors propose using rapid cooling to obtain a random solid solution for ductility, followed by aging at elevated temperatures to induce LCO for strength. They suggest that the variability in LCO offers a new knob for property tuning in single-phase alloys.
quotes: The LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities.
The shear stress required to drive forward a leading partial dislocation needs to increase by as much as a factor of three, when an RSS has been annealed at 650 K to increase LCO.

item.research_question: How does local chemical order (LCO) affect local dislocation segment activation barriers in multi-principal element alloys?
item.material_system: Multi-principal element alloys (specifically samples with equilibrium LCOs at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K)
item.processing_route: Hybrid MD and MC simulations on 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm samples (30 samples per condition) at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K; quenched to 0 K; cylinder configurations (20 nm diameter, 10 nm length) cut with a partial dislocation of screw character introduced; quasi-static athermal shearing employed; MEPs calculated using the simplified and improved string method with FIRE algorithm (reparameterization every 10 increments, convergence <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations)
item.test_conditions: Temperatures of 650 K, 950 K, and 1350 K for equilibrium LCO; 0 K for energy minimization; athermal stress limit via quasi-static shearing
key_findings: 30 different samples were obtained for each processing condition to ensure meaningful statistics
Sample dimensions were 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm along x[11¯0], y[1¯1¯1¯], and z[112¯]
Cylinder configurations had a diameter of 20 nm and axial direction along [112¯]
Dislocation line length was 10 nm as detrapping processes are on the nanoscale
Outer layers of atoms with thickness >2x potential cutoff radius were fixed during energy minimization
Inner cylindrical region with 10 nm diameter was used to calculate average local shear stress
Convergence criterion for MEP calculation was displacement <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations
item.mechanism: The authors employed hybrid MD and MC simulations to obtain equilibrium LCOs and then used the string method to calculate minimum energy pathways (MEPs) for dislocation segments, aiming to examine LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers.
quotes: In order to examine the LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers, hybrid MD and MC simulations were performed
For meaningful statistics, 30 different samples were obtained for each processing condition
MEPs were then calculated using the simplified and improved string method
